Brain organoids derived from human pluripotent stem cells matured on a schedule that tracked gestational age in vivo, as measured by transcriptional signatures. Single-cell RNA sequencing at days 30, 60, 120, and 200 revealed sequential emergence of progenitors, deep-layer neurons, upper-layer neurons, and astrocytes, matching the order seen in fetal tissue. Pseudotime analysis estimated a developmental clock with a correlation of r = 0.91 to a reference atlas. Chemical perturbation of the clock — using an inhibitor of a chromatin-modifying enzyme — accelerated maturation without altering cell-type proportions, suggesting that timing is controlled by epigenetic mechanisms and not only by extrinsic signals. Electrophysiological recordings confirmed emergent network oscillations after day 150.
